questions.q: What is the capstone business process this chapter builds across all three lessons?
options: A generic ticket auto-close process with no branching or approvals
Contractor Offboarding: revoking access, confirming equipment return, and creating an IT disable-account task when a contract ends
A brand-new hire onboarding checklist
A password reset self-service flow
questions.explain: Contractor Offboarding is the scenario chosen because it genuinely needs several of the course's core mechanisms working together.

questions.q: Why is a Scheduled trigger the right choice for firing when a contractor's end date arrives, rather than a Record trigger?
options: Record triggers cannot read date fields at all
Scheduled triggers are always faster to configure than Record triggers
The end date field was set weeks earlier and nothing changes on the record the day it actually matters, so the flow has to proactively check for the date arriving
A Record trigger would fire too many times per day
questions.explain: A Record trigger fires on insert/update — but nothing updates the contractor record on the day the end date actually arrives, so a recurring Scheduled trigger that queries for matching dates is needed instead.

questions.q: In the flow sketch for this capstone, why does the If/Else branch on contractor_type come before the access-revocation step?
options: The branch has no real purpose in this flow and could be removed
If/Else steps must always be the first step in any flow
Contractor type determines which manager gets assigned the approval
IT contractors and non-IT contractors have different systems to revoke access from, so the branch determines which revocation path applies
questions.explain: The branch exists because the two contractor types need different access-revocation handling before the flow continues.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes the access-revocation step a strong candidate for a subflow rather than inline flow logic?
options: Subflows are required for every step that follows an If/Else
It works the same way regardless of which branch reached it, making it reusable — the same test Lesson 13 used for subflow candidates
Inline logic cannot call other actions
Access revocation always requires a separate flow scope
questions.explain: A step that's identical no matter how you got there, and that could be reused elsewhere, is exactly the pattern Lesson 13 identified as subflow-worthy.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend sketching the flow's steps in plain language before opening Flow Designer?
options: Flow Designer requires a written sketch to be uploaded before it will save a flow
Sketching is only useful for flows with no branching
It replaces the need to choose a trigger type
So the build in Flow Designer follows a plan instead of becoming trial and error inside the canvas
questions.explain: The sketch is design work done up front specifically so Lesson 26's actual build goes faster and more deliberately.
